content: Adenoids, also known as pharyngeal tonsils or nasopharyngeal tonsils, are a collection of lymphoid tissue located at the very back of the nasal cavity, in the roof of the nasopharynx, where the nasal passages transition into the throat. In children, they typically form a soft mound in the roof and posterior wall of the nasopharynx, positioned just above and behind the uvula. Adenoids are an integral part of the immune system. Like other lymphoid tissues, they function by trapping infectious agents such as viruses and bacteria and producing antibodies to combat these pathogens. Due to their location at the back of the nasal airway, adenoids play a role in defending the body against inhaled substances. However, their immune function diminishes with age as the adenoids naturally shrink. By late childhood, adenoids usually regress significantly, which is why problems associated with enlarged adenoids are uncommon in adults. When adenoids become enlarged, a condition known as adenoid hypertrophy, they can grow to a size comparable to a ping pong ball and may completely obstruct airflow through the nasal passages. Even if the enlargement is not severe enough to fully block the nasal airway, it can still impede airflow to the extent that nasal breathing becomes laborious, forcing the individual to breathe through an open mouth instead. Enlarged adenoids can also partially obstruct the nasal airway in a way that alters the voice, even without entirely stopping nasal airflow. The surgical removal of adenoids is referred to as an adenoidectomy. This procedure is typically performed under general anesthesia (or less commonly, local anesthesia) through the mouth. The adenoids are removed using techniques such as curettage, cauterization, laser ablation, or other methods of tissue ablation. Histologically, adenoids differ from other types of tonsils. They are lined with pseudostratified columnar epithelium and lack the crypts that are characteristic of other tonsillar tissues. Adenoids are often removed in conjunction with the palatine tonsils, a procedure that can result in a very sore throat for approximately a week and may cause unpleasant breath during the recovery period. While adenoids typically become functionally redundant after the age of three, they must be removed if they cause significant problems, although in many cases, they naturally shrink over time.
